messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 67

He is a 55-year-old painter, a man whose hands once moved with quiet purpose across canvas—broad strokes of ochre and umber, the careful blending of sky into sea. He has a workshop behind his house, where the smell of turpentine and linseed oil used to mix with the sound of his son’s laughter. That was before.

The trauma happened eighteen months ago. His son, a twenty-three-year-old mechanic, was killed in a hit-and-run while walking home from a friend’s house. The phone call came at 11:47 p.m.—a policeman’s voice, flat and official. He remembers the hallway tiles, the way his knees hit the floor, the phone still in his hand. He did not cry then. He stood up, walked to the bedroom, and told his wife. Her scream is still embedded in the walls.

In the weeks that followed, he could not enter his studio. The sight of a half-finished painting—a portrait of his son that was meant to be a birthday gift—made his chest tighten until he could not breathe. He told his wife he would finish it later. He never did. Eventually he covered it with a white sheet, but even that does not help. Sometimes he walks past the studio door and feels a jolt, as if the room itself is dangerous.

He stopped painting entirely for six months. When he finally forced himself back—because the bills needed paying, because his wife looked at him with worry—his hands were different. They tremble now, especially when he tries to paint faces. He works only on abstract landscapes, and even then he avoids the color blue. Blue was his son’s favorite. The last time he accidentally mixed a cerulean tone, he had to leave the room, sweating, heart pounding, convinced he could hear his son’s voice calling his name from the next room.

He cannot drive past the intersection where the accident happened. On days when his route forces him near it, he takes a long detour, arriving at job sites late and short-tempered. His wife has stopped asking him to go to the grocery store because he will return empty-handed, claiming they didn’t have what she wanted. She knows the truth: the store is on the same block as the bus stop where his son used to wait.

Sleep is a battlefield. He wakes three or four times a night, gasping from dreams that he cannot fully recall but that leave him with a metallic taste in his mouth and the sensation of cold glass against his cheek. He often sleeps in the guest room now, because his wife’s breathing sounds too much like his son’s did when he was a child with asthma. The guilt of that thought—that he cannot stand the sound of the woman he loves—makes him pull the blanket over his head.

He drinks. Not heavily, but regularly. Two beers after dinner, sometimes three on weekends. The alcohol dulls the edge of the intrusive images: his son’s face in the casket, the police officer’s badge catching the light, the moment he had to identify the body. He did not look for long. But he saw enough. That image plays in a loop, especially when he tries to be still.

He has not cried since that first night. He told me during our third session: “Tears are for children. My son is gone. What good do tears do now?” His jaw is always tight. He clenches his fists when he talks about the driver who was never caught. He has thought about finding him. He has thought about revenge. That frightens him more than the nightmares.

His wife tells him he is not the same man she married. He knows she is right. The man who used to whistle while scraping his palette, the man who teased his son about his greasy fingernails—that man is buried somewhere beneath the debris of that November night. He still goes to work, still paints walls and ceilings for clients, but the joy is gone. It is just motion now, muscle memory, a body going through the rituals of a life that no longer feels like his own.
